Will the US govt want to take a 10% strategic stake in NVDA? 

2. Export controls have “worked” insofar as having slowed down China’s AI development. Without access to the most advanced GPUs, China has to spend time and money to reinvent key technologies that already exist in the U.S. before embarking on the multi-trillion parameters models. To Jensen’s credit, this delay isn’t free but may be bought at the expense of spurring a Chinese AI hardware-software ecosystem that’s eventually entirely independent of NVidia. That would be bad for NVidia and he argues also for the US technological dominance.

It seems that indeed may be the case bc “NVidia isn’t a car company” that’s easily substitutable but a sticky and powerful ecosystem or OS. Except to Jensen’s critics, that’s also exactly why they want to limit China’s access to it. China was always going to try to build a NVidia tech stack replica from CUDA to the interconnect software like NVLink or NIXL. Delaying China by a few months or a couple years is exactly the goal the proponents of the export controls are after. At that point, as I said in a post yesterday, the difference stems from a difference in existential values.

Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

Tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. ET, October PCE inflation and the revised Q3 GDP figure land together. I’m watching silver’s reaction to a softer inflation reading in particular. If yields fall and silver still struggles to hold $40, that would tell me sellers have more to unload.

“Jevon’s paradox stopped working for AI in the past 2 months” - Ramp

This is the sole reason the AI infra trade is down -40%. 

Supply is known and coming. 

The token price cuts have always led to a disproportionately higher increase in demand for tokens, aka Jevon’s paradox. 

Which means in plain English, revenue go up fast, because cheaper intelligence = new use cases. 

But recently, to the surprise of many people, that stopped happening. Which is very bad for stocks that rely on rapidly increasing token demand. 

It signals that for the first time in the AI trade that the supply of tokens is finally outpacing the demand. 

Supply > demand 
= price down 

The big question is when do new use cases emerge that reignite a new demand cycle of Jevon’s Paradox? 

The reason to be particularly concerned is this slowdown is happening before compute supply triples over the next 2 years.  

Personally, I think longterm it’s possible for token demand to absorb all of this new supply and some. But it’s heavily reliant on the slope of model capability leaps unlocking more economically valuable tasks. 

If that stalls, then it’ll be harder to absorb all the incoming supply. If it accelerates, it’ll be easier.

OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

Six months ago, I would have thought that specialist models in biology would be outperforming frontier LLMs until we scale things up by another couple orders of magnitude. My median estimate for when something like this would happen would have probably been 2030. 

Instead, our generalist language models, today, are performing tasks at or above the state-of-the-art in various protein design & understanding tasks. And there is clear improvement across all domains as our models improve generally.

The implications of this are enormous - we are on the doorstep of being able to program biology using natural language.

Funnily enough, even Ethereum seems likely to adopt the post-quantum signature scheme that was developed by Bitcoin developers out of @Blockstream research. The scheme looks more and more likely to be enshrined in Bitcoin's consensus code every day that goes by—with a full security analysis published by the team just last week. 

More importantly, there is shockingly little contention around this scheme (outside of an appropriate level of tradeoff/risk assessment) since the scheme specification was published in September.  

It is literally an insiders' joke, that the core dev community has become "nerd-sniped" by quantum, and the mailing list has become a post-quantum silo. Even @nic_carter has acknowledged the sharp shift in tone over the last year. He may even take credit for it, and tbh, he might deserve some.

For additional clarity on developers' posture around quantum—I'm not exaggerating when I say *the majority* of the most prominent Bitcoin developers in the world are now working on quantum, with many funded full time or, at a minimum, regularly engaged in serious review on the mailing list and other forums. 

Many of these developers have completely halted other projects to focus exclusively on Quantum... or AI-relevant security, which thank God is also getting the attention it deserves right now. 

This all to say, the developers seem more than capable of "making a decision" on this one—this take is about as stale as sour milk.
